title: Emergent Order Parameters of Allostery: An AI Framework for Predicting and Engineering Protein Regulation
scientific_merit_and_innovation_justific:
While the general topic of allostery is interesting,
the scale of the proposed investigations does not go beyond
individual proteins, rather than mesoscale dynamics. The
general idea is to use AI to analyze simulated molecules in order
to find and predict allosteric pathways. There is a possibility this
could work, but the potential for providing meaningful results is
unclear. The methodology is quite vague, making it difficult to
gauge the potential significance of the results.
feasibility_justification:
The team will generate large number of
simulations, which will be supported by Folding@Home. The
simulations are likely to be completed on time. It would appear
that implementing their AI methods should also be
straightforward. There are no concerns about the timline.
data_sources_and_limitations_justificati:
It is not clear if the available simulated trajectories
are sufficient, which would be necessary to make this a synthesis
project. There is no description provided for the duration of
available trajectories, and what timescales would be needed for
the analysis to be effective. There also appears to be a rather
large body of new data that will be generated, in the form of new
simulations, rather than relying on existing data sets.
open_science_compliance_justification:
The proposal directly indicates that open-source
software will be generated. However, there is no discussion of
reproducibility, hence the lower rating.
overall_rating_summary:
Overall, the team aims to address an interesting
topic, namely allostery in proteins. However, there have been
decades of effort dedicated to exploring allostery. Accordingly,
there is a significant chance that the proposed efforts will not be
able to yield major advances in this crowded area of research.
Enthusiasm would be greater if the proposed research area was
less developed, where there could be more opportunities for
novel contributions.
Despite the crowded field, with the accessibility of AI/ML
techniques, there is room for these techniques to possibly
provide insights. However, it is common for AI/ML efforts to be
rather poorly defined, which frequently leads to results that
have little significance. Based on the level of detail provided in
the proposal, it is not clear whether this particular strategy is
likely to provide significant insights, or not.

allostery really works” using machine learning, with the goal of
establishing a framework for obtaining “order parameters.” The
group wishes that the outcome here will allow them to classify,
predict, engineer receptor behaviors.

poised to advance our understanding of how we should perceive
and study protein allostery in this AI era.
The approach is multi-layered and rigorous, building upon their
track record and recent findings.

title: From Protein Knots to Pierced Lassos: Unraveling the Evolutionary Origin of Complex Topologies
scientific_merit_and_innovation_justific:
This is an interesting proposal on a timely problem.
The combination of structural biology, proteomics, and
phylogenetics of proteins with complex knotted structures to
study the emergence of these properties on evolutionary
timescales is exciting and innovative. I believe the project will
lead to new and important insights into protein evolution with
many applications. The proposed methodology logical and
appropriate.
feasibility_justification:
The goals and milestones seem realistic for the
overall project plan and the timeline.
data_sources_and_limitations_justificati: I believe that the tools and data the investigators propose to use are appropriate. I think that this project has great potential, although there could be a stronger vision for their approach to synthesize and interpret the information that they collect in an evolutionary context/
open_science_compliance_justification:
Although it is clear that the research requires a
commitment to open, team, and reproducible science principles,
there is little written in the proposal to specifically demonstrate
how they will ensure these practices.
overall_rating_summary:
This is an interesting proposal on an exciting, novel,
and timely topic of wide interest to biologists, and one that
requires an interdisciplinary effort and true synthesis of
different data types and knowledge. The project is innovative in
its focus on knotted protein structures, and combining structural
biology, proteomics, and phylogenetics to study the evolution of
these structures. The team has diverse expertise that seems well
equipped to process and understand large-scale protein data. I
think that the team is likely to provide new and important
insights into protein evolution with many applications. The
proposed methodology is largely appropriate.
However, there are some aspects that could be clarified and
improved to maximize the impact of the project. I was looking
for more information about their plans to synthesize information
to provide deep insights. The analysis of protein structures in a
phylogenetic framework will give them important insights into
when events occur, but the proposal would be stronger with
more details about how they will provide insights into protein
innovation and function. The addition of the investigators from
the University of Kentucky helps with this, but the team could deepen their expertise in evolutionary analysis to ensure that they can extract rich information and synthesize new knowledge about the evolution of these proteins.

title: From Protein Knots to Pierced Lassos: Unraveling the Evolutionary Origin of Complex Topologies
scientific_merit_and_innovation_justific:
The evolutionary origin of complex protein
topologies (knots, slipknots, pierced lassos, etc.) is an
understudied phenomenon, and its investigation merits support
as this may reveal previously unappreciated phenomena in the
field of protein structure/function. However, there exists the
possibility that such complex topologies do not have any specific
functional consequences. That is, they may have occurred in the
course of protein evolution and have been carried along, not
because they conferred any special function or benefit, but
simply because they were not detrimental to organismal
survival. It is not clear from the proposal to what extent this
latter scenario may be a possibility and how it would be
incorporated into the scope of the proposal.
feasibility_justification:
The proposal anticipates two publications over the
course of the 24-month project timeline. This appears to be an
attainable goal within the timeframe and resources of the
project
data_sources_and_limitations_justificati:
It is unclear to what extent the project will rely on
experimentally determined topologies versus purely
computationally predicted topologies. In the case of
computationally predicted topologies, it is unclear to what
extent errors in computational prediction are likely and how
much those errors might affect the planned work, especially if
the errors are not easily detectable.
open_science_compliance_justification: No concerns
overall_rating_summary:
A key strength of the proposal is the synthesis of
existing databases to probe the evolutionary origin of complex
protein topologies, which is a relatively understudied
phenomenon. The project participants cover a wide range of
topics in science and mathematics that are relevant to the
project. A compelling plan for productive management and
synthesis of this expertise is lacking, including what specific
contributions from NCEMS staff will augment the capacity of the
team. It is not clear what the implications to the project goals are
if complex topologies do not generally have specific functional
consequences. The reliance on computationally predicted
structures increases the overall level of risk.

title: Deciphering systemic biological networks through AI-driven multi-omic integration
scientific_merit_and_innovation_justific: This proposal directly addresses emergent phenomena by studying inter-organ cross talks at the whole-organism level and proposing to identify organ-specific emergent properties. The PIs propose to implement a reaction-diffusion model based neural network, which is highly innovative. If successful, this can provide a new system-level physiological understanding and advance the field. The proposed generation of digital “twin rat” is also highly innovative, as it could establish a new in silico testbed. While the mathematical framework of the methodology is clear, the proposal lacks some key methodological details. Specifically, the PIs did not explain how the initial graph structure representing organ-to-organ connectivity will be determined, what strategies will ensure comparability across seven different omic layers, and what validation metrics will be used to assess model accuracy and biological relevance.
feasibility_justification: Year 1 goals are achievable, but completing the full 18-organ interaction map by end of Year 2 seems overly ambitious given the complexity of integrating seven omic layers.
data_sources_and_limitations_justificati: The proposal clearly demonstrates a synthesis project, using the publicly available MoTrPAC dataset. This dataset is sufficient to carry out the proposed activities, as it contains multi omic measurements from 18 tissues across multiple time points from the same animals. The proposal appropriately identifies that using homogeneous data from the same animals addresses a major limitation of previous studies that relied on heterogeneous datasets. However, the proposal does not discuss potential limitations such as missing data across omic types, varying measurement frequencies, data quality issues, or batch effects.
open_science_compliance_justification: There is no explicit statement regarding open science principles. No plans for data sharing, code repositories, or reproducibility frameworks were mentioned.
overall_rating_summary: This proposal addresses fundamental questions about organ cross-talk and emergent properties in whole-organism physiology using innovative computational approaches applied to a publicly available dataset. The MoTrPAC dataset is well-suited for this synthesis work, and the proposed computational framework is essential for integrating multi-omic data across organs and time to reveal system-level regulatory networks. The interdisciplinary team is well-qualified and the potential scientific impact is substantial. However, the proposal contains insufficient technical detail on model implementation and validation strategies. The Year 2 timeline seems too ambitious. Additionally, no explicit commitment to open science principles, data sharing, or reproducibility practices was provided.

title: Conserved Disorder: Learning Sequence Conservation from Functional Constraints in Intrinsically Disordered Regions
scientific_merit_and_innovation_justific:
The goal of this proposal is to create a database of
‘relatively conserved IDRs’ that we can use to further probe IDPs
on a computational (and experimental?) approach. A big
component of the proposal uses established databases to mine
these data. A nice two-part plan is presented to (1) comb the
databases for IDRs that are well-studied (e.g., deep mutational
scanning) and for which info is present regarding conserved
motifs and PTMs, and (2) to use these databases and motif
prediction tools to scan through the whole IDRome and
construct a proteome-scale map of IDRs under functional
constraint. This is a significant problem as the IDR field is now
aiming to dissect the key molecular grammar features of IDRs –
there is a need to identify candidates for further study. Some
weaknesses concern novelty as other groups are identifying
molecular grammar of IDR sequences or finding new ways to
identify conservation of IDRs (through both sequence and
structural properties). It would be helpful to find ways to assess
their goal of establishing this new ‘conserved’ IDR database and
cross-validating it, as well as to compare their approach with
other teams’ approaches on examining IDR properties and
linkage to function.
Rigor is present, although it’s hard to know how the data will be
experimentally assessed as few details are presented on that
end.While experiments are not a focus of NCEMS proposals, the
inclusion of experiments would strengthen this application.
Another weakness concerns the likelihood that many IDRs have
diverse functions, so linking some of their work to specific
biological functions of IDRs may be challenging.
feasibility_justification:
Yes, I the goals and milestones are realistic given
some preliminary data presented, and existing connections with
folks at NCEMS.
data_sources_and_limitations_justificati:
The proposal describes a project that takes
advantages of multiple state-of-the-art resources to characterize
proteins. The combination of the databases will likely yield
targets for further study. The data sources (both in the main
proposal and in the alternative approaches) are sufficient to
carry out their plan.
open_science_compliance_justification:
I believe that this is present within the proposal but
it is not clearly stated aside from “Continued support will enable
development of scalable bioinformatics pipelines, metadata
integration, and reproducible computational frameworks.”
Strengths from this proposal do include the team aspect of the
work as the group includes leaders in the IDP/IDR field. Aside
from making the conserved IDR database available, it’s not
explicitly stated what the commitment is towards these
principles, e.g., how reproducibility will be incorporated into
their strategies.
overall_rating_summary:
This is a timely proposal that addresses a need to
find ‘conserved’ IDRs and build a library for continued study.
The question of relating specific intrinsically disordered protein
(IDP) sequences to function is a difficult one. Part of the reason
why this is challenging is that IDP/IDR sequences are not well-
conserved in the traditional way that structured/well-folded
sequences are. Therefore, the IDP field needs better tools and
computational analyses. Score-driving strengths are (1) a strong
team with established track records in the IDP field, (2)
preliminary data with the NCEMS team, (3) integration of
several databases and computational approaches including
machine learning. Some weaknesses concern (a) evaluating their
strategy against others, and (b) what if it is not easy to find
specific patterns in sequence or biophysical properties that lead
to function? Having obtained some of the preliminary data is
helpful but coupling this with predicted features could be
challenging given that we’re still trying to understand how to
predict these features in IDPs/IDRs such as SLiMs

title: Conserved Disorder: Learning Sequence Conservation from Functional Constraints in Intrinsically Disordered Regions
scientific_merit_and_innovation_justific:
This proposal addresses the very important
question of how sequence encodes function in intrinsically
disordered proteins. This has been a long standing question that
has grown in importance with the recent discovery of more and
more disordered proteins and the emergence of protein
condensates in our understanding of cell biology. The research
plan is simple, direct, and makes sense. The work is likely to
have an important impact, even if it were to achieve a fraction of
its aims. The only weakness, which is minor, is what the PI’s
mean when they talk about “function”. There is a lack of
specificity around this idea, which varies fundamental from one
protein to the next. As such it may be difficult to know how to
gauge the success of the work, when the protein functions are
themselves emerging and ill defined. This issue could be
addressed by limiting the scope of the work to a set of protein
that all have similar functions such as transcription factors or
fusion oncoproteins or RNA binding proteins, etc.
feasibility_justification:
The goals are probably a bit too broad. However, I
still consider the proposal very good because the impact would
be high, even if a fraction of the goals were achieved.
data_sources_and_limitations_justificati:
I have limited knowledge of the databases that the
PI’s will bring together, but it is quite clear that they will bring
together diverse data sources in a true synthesis.
open_science_compliance_justification: The authors state the intention of creating an open source database. As someone in the IDR field, I can attest that it would be of great use the community.
overall_rating_summary:
See my statements in the first category. In brief, I
find the proposal very strong in terms of the merit of the idea
and the need from the community. The minor weakness I
identified above is that scope is rather large, such that what the
PI’s mean by the “function” of the proteins is somewhat unclear.
I see this as a minor issue that can be addressed by reducing the
scope, at least initially, to groups of IDR-containing protein with
a single or more constrained set of functions.

title: Integrative Multi-Omics Synthesis to Identify Shared Molecular Mechanisms of Mammalian Hibernation
scientific_merit_and_innovation_justific:
The team proposes a cross-species analysis of gene expression during active hibernation in mammals. They will leverage extensive publicly available datasets across tissues and
species. They will use innovative phylogenetic gene expression
modeling approaches that have not yet been applied to address
the proposed problem. The proposal addresses and important,
unsolved problem (relevant to metabolic disorders and deeper
understanding of mammalian physiology). Their work is
appropriately responsive to the emergent phenomena call.
Weaknesses: While the modeling approaches were innovative
and interesting, I fear that there will be several issues arising during the analysis that may need alternative approaches - these were not addressed in the proposal. For example: How will differences in expression across tissues be analyzed within species and across species (i.e. how will their methods account for missing data)? They mention this at the end of the introduction but then do not revisit it explicitly later in the proposal. Furthermore, how will the team handle non-orthologous genes (unique signatures)? (they only describe their approach to assess convergently expressed genes). When were the RNA-seq data taken during hibernation across the datasets?
Timing matters when it comes to circadian phenomena…How will they handle issues of spice variants across tissues with species and across species? How will they address incomplete experimental designs in which gene expression in different tissues is measured in different species (See Data Sources
Table)? How will technical batch effects be handled (to differentiate true biological effects from technical noise)?
Minor weakness: What will criteria be for “orthology” (% identity, etc?) How will important phylogenetic signals of
convergent gene expression of unknown function (i.e. falling outside GO ontology annotations) be analyzed or interpreted?
feasibility_justification:
Strong justification for the timeline and feasibility.
If everything goes according to plan, the project is reasonable
and plan is doable in the allotted time frame. However, the
potential pitfalls (see above) may significantly delay progress.
data_sources_and_limitations_justificati:
Although the data sources and associated genomes
are available and annotated, the issue of different tissues and
time points being measured for gene expression across
organisms is not addressed. One would expect substantial
differences in different tissue types at different time points
during hibernation.
open_science_compliance_justification:
The proposal says they are committed to open
science (part 8), but they don’t say how. How will the models,
analyses, and other aspects of proposal results be shared with
the public? How will the models be stored / archived long-term
to avoid deprecation? Will they publish in open-source journals?
overall_rating_summary:
Although the team, need for NCEMS support, and publicly
available datasets and cybrainfrastructure are strong, additional
rationale and alternative approaches for known pitfalls of
integration of data with incomplete experimental designs across
studies is needed (different tissue types, missing data,
alternative splicing, etc).

title: Integrative Multi-Omics Synthesis to Identify Shared Molecular Mechanisms of Mammalian Hibernation
scientific_merit_and_innovation_justific:
The proposal seeks to address how variations in
gene expression programs in hibernating organisms lead to
emergent shifts in those organisms phylogenies. The use of high

title: Revealing the Ontology of Allostery through Community-Scale Synthesis
scientific_merit_and_innovation_justific:
The proposal aims to connect allostery in
transporter proteins to specific sequence sites and create
evolutionary landscapes, which is highly significant. While the
proposal does not include specific details on its connection to
mesoscale, by comparing allosteric and non-allosteric homologs,
the project will trace how small sequence changes accumulate to
create emergent regulatory networks. I find the approach
rigorous, as the methodology is grounded in established
practices (ASMD, SCA, DCA) and will also use emerging ones
(LGL and AI for spot prediction); however reliance on domain
insertion as a proxy and focus on metal-binding may limit
generality.
feasibility_justification:
The goals and milestones are realistic for the 2-year

manageable, though scaling to 50 families could be ambitious if
data sparsity arises.

it integrates diverse databases (sequence, structure, mutations)
to create a new data base, which will then be analyzed.
Limitations are also acknowledged, as lack of negative examples,
data sparsity and annotations standards.
open_science_compliance_justification:
The team will make the database publically
available and plans to publish the dataset.

The proposal aims to understand the evolutionary
origin of allostery in transporter proteins and assemble a
database that will help cataloguing the degree of allostery in this
class of proteins. It has two main aims: to identify amino acids
sites responsible with allostery and to establish their
evolutionary origins. Strengths include rigorous multifaced
approach and a diverse team, while its focus on metal-binding
transporters and the use of domain-insertion as proxy for
allostery are areas for improvement.

title: Revealing the Ontology of Allostery through Community-Scale Synthesis
scientific_merit_and_innovation_justific:
This proposal tackles a long-standing critical
knowledge gap: the structural origins of allostery in proteins.
The approach to gaining insight is not necessarily particularly
new, as it builds on the very strong previous work in this area by
the collaborative team, but the proposed synthesis offers the
potential to generate immediate and long-term impact. The
identification of systems with varying levels of allostery will be a
major improvement in the available information for analysis
both for the investigative team and the broader community. The
main thing that cools my enthusiasm is the choice of focusing
exclusively on a large family of related membrane proteins. That
choice is likely to limit the generality of the insights gained due
to the stark differences between the thermodynamics of
membrane protein structure and dynamics as compared to that
of soluble proteins. Great insights are likely for the class of
proteins chosen, but the project would have greater impact if
multiple classes were studied that range between cellular
environments.
feasibility_justification:
The goals and timeline seem appropriate and well
justified. The team has the necessary expertise to achieve the
proposed timeline.
data_sources_and_limitations_justificati:
Data sources are identified and there is a clear
emphasis on synthesis across data types (sequence alignments
to examine evolutionary relationships coupled with molecular
dynamics to examine networks). It is not clear how much data is
expected to come from each source, but given that collection of
the data is a main initial goal, that’s understandable. It is a little
unclear to me how simulating 50-100 proteins will compare to
the number of proteins that will be examined in the evolutionary
analysis, nor the extent to which sufficient statistical sampling
will be achieved from the proposed data sets.
open_science_compliance_justification:
This aspect is only really addressed insofar as
proposing to make the resulting database available via CYVERSE
and ‘open to community augmentation’. It’s not clear to me what
that means in terms of it being accessible for analysis and or
allowing the community to contribute new data, nor how such
contributions would be curated going forward. Being part of
CYVERSE should mean that the approach will comply with open
science principles. Reproducibility was not explicitly addressed
in the proposal.
overall_rating_summary:
The proposed project has the potential to fill a
major hole in our understanding of allostery while also creating
a much-needed data resource. My enthusiasm for the project is
only limited by the choice to focus on a family of membrane
proteins. This choice, in my view, will limit the generalizability of
the findings from the proposed analysis. That being said, if
successful, the approach used in this project has the potential to
be a model for building similar databases and analyses for other
classes of proteins for which the rules governing allostery and
evolution of allosteric mechanisms may be different from
membrane proteins in important ways due to differences in
cellular environment and the thermodynamic impacts thereof (e.g. soluble cytosolic proteins, peripheral membrane proteins,
nuclear proteins, etc.).
The team is excellent and has the relevant expertise to give the
project a high potential for success. The need for NCEMS
resources is clear, and the timeline and use of NCEMS resources
are laid out nicely.

title: Revealing the Ontology of Allostery through Community-Scale Synthesis
scientific_merit_and_innovation_justific:
The goal of this proposal is to trace the
evolutionary origins of allostery in a defined class of proteins, P-
type membrane transporters. The idea for this database that
differs from those in the past is that it will compare both
transporters that contain allosteric sites to non-allosteric family
members to generate the ‘allosterome’. This seems like an
interesting and important question in biology with many long-
term applications, making it a relevant and worthy topic of
study. To my knowledge, this work is novel as there is no other
dataset that compares allosteric vs non-allosteric proteins of this
type. In terms of approach, the proposal is very brief and rather
light on details for how the evolutionary analysis will be
performed. A more complete description of this aspect of the
proposal would have been appreciated.
feasibility_justification:
The overall scope of the work and proposed in this
2-year timeline appears feasible. The data products section
covers the outputs for this proposal. The detailed timeline for
each phase of the project is well described and appears
reasonable.
data_sources_and_limitations_justificati:
There is an extensive list of data sources provided
that will give a robust set of initial data to consider. However, the
biggest caveat to the proposal is the fact that it there could be
mis- classifications of proteins as non-allosteric. If there is no
current evidence that a protein is allosterically regulated, it will
be included in this category but that does not necessarily mean
that allosteric regulation will not one day be discovered. Thus,
while the negative control dataset is very interesting in this
proposal, it is hard to ensure that a given protein lacks this
particular mode of regulation. This could lead to mis-

title: SynEvo: Discovering Evolutionary Principles of Molecular Organization through Cross-Species Data Synthesis
scientific_merit_and_innovation_justific:
This team proposes to integrate population-level
genomic variation with multi-omic (transcriptomic, proteomic,
metabolomic) data to understand how genetic variation and
pathway flux produce conserved mesoscale modules. Their
machine-learning based approach will be constrained by
knowledge of metabolic pathways and flux and will use
“interpretable” ML methods so that results will have meaning
and not just a black-box output. The proposed methodology is
clear and has strong potential to advance knowledge.
feasibility_justification:
The timeline appears to be feasible, and the
proposal includes detailed contingencies in the event that the
pace is slower than expected. Even if the team must rely on the
contingencies, the expected output would be significant (i.e.
limited to human data and not mosquito). My only minor
concern is how to harmonize the data from the diverse sources.
There is not much detail given in the proposal (though the length
limit does preclude a full description).
data_sources_and_limitations_justificati:

genomic and multi-omic data. The Pis clearly describe the goal of
synthesizing these data to produce an understanding of
mesoscale phenomena.

be made public and version controlled. Furthermore, the
harmonized data sets will be made publicly available with DOIs.

use of multiscale data to understand how genetic variation leads
to conserved mesoscale modules while also enabling
evolutionary innovation. The PIs describe the use of a number of
existing data sets along with interpretable and biologically-
constrained ML methods for their analysis. I did have minor
concerns about the roles of the NCEMS staff and the students,

While it is stated that variational autoencoders would be used to learn joint embeddings of genetic variation data and molecular states constrained by metabolic or gene regulatory networks, how the constraints would be applied has not been specified, however briefly. How many layers or parameters have not been specified; it isn’t clear where the estimates of 200K CPU and 300K GPU hours come from. Most importantly, the proposal lacks a clear statement of what would be learnt from the embeddings.3. It is claimed that the ML models would be interpretable. What kind of in silico experiments would be performed to interpret, or whether the model has a particular structure/parameterization amenable to interpretation, has not been specified.4. The choice of species has not been justified. Why mosquitos and not Drosophila, which has far more tissue-specific and species-specific data? There is no metabolomic data for mosquitos. Mosquitos have ATAC-Seq data, but no ATAC-Seq data have been mentioned for humans.5. There is a disconnect between the methodology specified in goal 3, the mapping of the embedding of the genetic variation/molecular states of one species to that of another, and the stated goal of identifying conserved, co-evolved, or novel “modules”. overall_rating_summary: Strengths: The goals of the proposal are valiant and could have a large impact on a wide range of scientific disciplines not just limited to molecular and cellular biosciences, but also in physics, chemistry, biology, data science, pharmaceutical sciences, etc. Determining and predicting the structure and dynamics of proteins and enzymes has been one of the biggest difficulties in advancing our knowledge in these fields, and major efforts have been dedicated to understanding these areas of research. In addition, the researchers are an excellent team of scientists with expertise in areas required for the proposed research, and a collaboration such as this is vital for advancing our knowledge in protein structure and dynamics and utilizing AI models to their full potential.Areas for improvement: Although I have no doubt the scientists are experts/have the expertise to carry out the proposed students, the methodology was not presented in a clear manner. As someone who understands biomolecular structure and dynamics well, I am unfamiliar with much of the computational acronyms, programs, and “jargon” that were used ubiquitously throughout the proposal. So I would have to take them at their word as to whether this would work or not.The main computational program the group will utilize, MD4PLM, has not been published on yet, and how the program works and is validated is unclear.The researchers state they have applied their own model, MD4PLM, to predict benchmarks for protein function prediction, but no results or conclusions from these preliminary studies were mentioned. They show data for “time-lagged independent component analysis visualization of a protein’s conformational landscape,” but there is no explanation as to what this means. Showing a figure of dots with no axes, labels, details of the experiment, or explanation of what a landscape even is not helpful or informative. They list numbers for parameters obtained from a modeling framework they developed, but the numbers/parameters, such as Fmax from GO-BP, EC, and GO-MF, and AUPRC, and what they represent are not explained, and therefore it is difficult to determine the advantages of the framework. One of the major aims of the proposal is to “utilize multimodal learning techniques recently developed in PI Chen’s lab,” but it is not clear what these techniques are. Is this the MD4PLM? I assume it is, but it was never explicitly stated.The key questions to be addressed by the project are a bit vague and unclear. I’m not sure how these studies will be able to link enzyme functions with dynamics. Is it predicted that enzymes with similar functions also have similar dynamics? This is not true with many enzyme classes. And will the studies actually be able to answer the questions “How can simulation-derived dynamics most effectively improve function prediction?” and “How to design an AI model to best leverage available simulations data and enhanced sampling techniques?” These seem like questions that are better asked after the researchers determine if their simulation-derived dynamics techniques effectively improve function prediction and leverage data already available.A brief explanation as to why the researchers selected specific “identified enzymes” for their initial experiments would be valuable. No specific enzymes or enzyme classes are mentioned in the proposal itself.

[Overall Rating | Score: 3.0]
Strengths: The goals of the proposal are valiant and could have a large impact on a wide range of scientific disciplines not just limited to molecular and cellular biosciences, but also in physics, chemistry, biology, data science, pharmaceutical sciences, etc. Determining and predicting the structure and dynamics of proteins and enzymes has been one of the biggest difficulties in advancing our knowledge in these fields, and major efforts have been dedicated to understanding these areas of research. In addition, the researchers are an excellent team of scientists with expertise in areas required for the proposed research, and a collaboration such as this is vital for advancing our knowledge in protein structure and dynamics and utilizing AI models to their full potential.Areas for improvement: Although I have no doubt the scientists are experts/have the expertise to carry out the proposed students, the methodology was not presented in a clear manner. As someone who understands biomolecular structure and dynamics well, I am unfamiliar with much of the computational acronyms, programs, and “jargon” that were used ubiquitously throughout the proposal. So I would have to take them at their word as to whether this would work or not.The main computational program the group will utilize, MD4PLM, has not been published on yet, and how the program works and is validated is unclear.The researchers state they have applied their own model, MD4PLM, to predict benchmarks for protein function prediction, but no results or conclusions from these preliminary studies were mentioned. They show data for “time-lagged independent component analysis visualization of a protein’s conformational landscape,” but there is no explanation as to what this means. Showing a figure of dots with no axes, labels, details of the experiment, or explanation of what a landscape even is not helpful or informative. They list numbers for parameters obtained from a modeling framework they developed, but the numbers/parameters, such as Fmax from GO-BP, EC, and GO-MF, and AUPRC, and what they represent are not explained, and therefore it is difficult to determine the advantages of the framework. One of the major aims of the proposal is to “utilize multimodal learning techniques recently developed in PI Chen’s lab,” but it is not clear what these techniques are. Is this the MD4PLM? I assume it is, but it was never explicitly stated.The key questions to be addressed by the project are a bit vague and unclear. I’m not sure how these studies will be able to link enzyme functions with dynamics. Is it predicted that enzymes with similar functions also have similar dynamics? This is not true with many enzyme classes. And will the studies actually be able to answer the questions “How can simulation-derived dynamics most effectively improve function prediction?” and “How to design an AI model to best leverage available simulations data and enhanced sampling techniques?” These seem like questions that are better asked after the researchers determine if their simulation-derived dynamics techniques effectively improve function prediction and leverage data already available.A brief explanation as to why the researchers selected specific “identified enzymes” for their initial experiments would be valuable. No specific enzymes or enzyme classes are mentioned in the proposal itself.

The methodological narrative relies on dense computational terminology that complicates broader scientific evaluation. Comprehensive assessment requires operational definitions for the proposed parameters alongside empirical validation for the MD4PLM platform and its associated preliminary figures.
rephrased_strengths: The project pursues impactful objectives capable of advancing multiple scientific disciplines including molecular biosciences and data science. The collaborative research team possesses the specific technical expertise required to execute the synthesis plan while ensuring open data access.
rephrased_weakness: The methodological narrative assumes broad familiarity with specific computational acronyms and advanced statistical parameters. Evaluating the MD4PLM software implementation necessitates accompanying validation metrics and theoretical justification for the targeted enzyme classes.

title: Integrating AI and Molecular Dynamics Simulations for Quantitative Prediction of Enzyme Functions
scientific_merit_and_innovation_justific: The proposal presents a strong, well-constructed plan to synthesize large-scale MD simulations, structural ensembles, and biophysical determinants using multimodal AI, directly addressing NCEMS’s core mission. By aggregating multi-resolution trajectories for about 10,000 enzymes and fusing them through the MD4PLM framework, the project aims to identify generalizable, emergent relationships between protein dynamics, energetics, and enzymatic function, a synthesis that would not be apparent from static data alone.The novelty is relatively high. The proposal combines all-atom, coarse-grained, and generative AI-MD with multimodal learning is innovative and has clear potential to advance protein function prediction. The rigor is also strong, with detailed plans for data curation, simulation pipelines, and benchmarking.A minor weakness is that the proposed work mostly focuses on individual enzymes rather than higher-order cellular systems, but the project clearly fits NCEMS’s broader objective of using data synthesis to reveal emergent biological insights.
feasibility_justification: The goals and milestones are ambitious but realistic for a two-year project. The team already has a functioning MD–AI framework, MD4PLM, and the plan leverages existing MD datasets, CG/AI-MD simulations. Computational benchmarks suggest the simulation targets are achievable with the requested resources. The scope is large, but the timeline is well structured and feasible with only minor concerns about data volume.
data_sources_and_limitations_justificati: The proposal clearly presents a data synthesis project, integrating large-scale MD simulations, structural databases, biophysical feature sets, and curated enzyme annotations into a unified multimodal framework. The data sources are comprehensive and appropriate for the project’s goals. The authors acknowledge key limitations, including restricted conformational sampling and variability across force fields, and propose reasonable mitigation strategies such as CG/AI-MD simulations, enhanced sampling, and cross-force-field validation. Minor concerns remain regarding the sheer scale of simulation data required, but overall the data identification and synthesis plan are strong and well justified.
open_science_compliance_justification: The proposal strongly commits to open and reproducible science. It plans to deposit all curated enzyme datasets, multi-resolution MD trajectories, and extracted biophysical determinants in open repositories such as MDRepo, Zenodo, and GitHub. The team also outlines plans for transparent data processing, public release of model benchmarks, and open-access publication.
overall_rating_summary: This is a strong and well-conceived synthesis project that aligns with NCEMS’s mission. The proposal leverages a capable, complementary team and builds on an already functional MD–AI framework, MD4PLM. The data sources are appropriate, the methodological plan is rigorous, and the computational needs are clearly justified. The commitment to open science is exemplary, and NCEMS support would substantially enhance the project’s scale and impact.Key strengths include strong preliminary results, a clear synthesis-oriented workflow, and the integration of multi-resolution MD data with advanced multimodal AI methods. The primary area for improvement is scope: the project is ambitious in volume, 10,000 proteins and extensive MD simulations, and while feasible, it would benefit from clearer prioritization or staged milestones to ensure manageability. Additionally, although the biological impact is meaningful, the proposal could more explicitly articulate how the synthesized datasets will reveal generalizable emergent principles beyond improved function prediction.

title: Discovery and functional analysis of bacterial organelles through mining and refinement of omics data
scientific_merit_and_innovation_justific: Strengths:The assembly of subcellular organelle structures in bacterial species is an exciting mesoscale molecular phenomenon and critically understudied. A more detailed understanding offers insights into the origins of these structures in eukaryotes.The breadth of structures examined here, BMC, ferrosomes, and condensates, presents an opportunity to identify novel categories of BMC-, ferrosome-, and condensate-associated genes.Use of gut microbiome multi-omic data offers a path to connecting subcellular organelle genes to their expression. While more challenging, there are opportunities to infer how production of these structures is regulated in their bacterial hosts.Weaknesses:The approach leverages known protein domains/families involved in BMCs, ferrosomes, and condensates. It is not clear how NCEMS resources would offer more than conventional bioinformatic searches for these domains in public data. More importantly, it is unclear how novel types of subcellular organelles will be discovered with this framework.Clearer justification for datasets is needed. The focus on gut microbiome datasets has some limitations. Arguably, there are few public microbiome datasets that offer the level of resolution across MAGs, transcriptomes, and proteomes. That said, there is scant evidence provided to support that there will be an abundance of subcellular organelle information in these datasets. Many of the well-characterized BMC and ferrosome systems studied are in bacteria not associated with the gut microbiome. Likewise, the domains used in the proposed analyses may miss novel BMC and ferrosome genes in the gut microbiome data. There is a reasonable likelihood that mining this extensive data will yield underpowered results to draw conclusions or formulate well-supported hypotheses to drive future research.Connecting production, or lack of production, of subcellular organelles, and their function, to specific stresses cannot be resolved with these data, as suggested in outcomes. The changes in the host gut environment across the different datasets are myriad. Pinpointing specific environmental parameters affecting organelle-producing bacteria may be possible using co-registered transcriptomic information in specific species; however, that is not elaborated.The collective focus on BMC, ferrosome, and condensates may be too broad to allow for meaningful discoveries. Each of these systems are structurally distinct and could be their own line of inquiry with this type of bioinformatic approach. Apart from being subcellular structures that occur in some bacterial species, there isn’t much describing how outcomes of this proposed work will provide a unifying perspective on why these structures are made and when we should expect organisms to produce them.
feasibility_justification: The proposed timeline for the analyses are reasonable given the datasets and bioinformatic tools/approaches described.
data_sources_and_limitations_justificati: There is synthesis of data across genomic, transcriptomic, and proteomic levels, but there is not obvious synthesis between the systems, BMC, ferrosome, condensates. Each appears to be a distinct line of inquiry.The selected gut microbiome datasets are likely data-rich, but there is a reasonable likelihood that there are limited numbers of subcellular organelle-producing taxa in the gut. Alternative datasets from environmental systems, soil and agriculture, are not considered for this approach. While many of these may lack higher-level omic data, many now contain MAGs and transcriptomic information.
open_science_compliance_justification: While the project will use public datasets, there is not a clear statement of how novel findings will be made open/available beyond peer-reviewed publications. There is significant subject expertise, but the mechanics of how these project leads will synthesize findings between subject areas, BMC, ferrosome, condensates, is not made clear.
overall_rating_summary: This project looks to identify genes associated with production of bacterial subcellular organelles in gut microbiome data and infer their patterns of regulation in response to varied host gut conditions. Using human gut microbiome multi-omics data, major proposed outcomes will be identification of subcellular organelle systems homologous to known organelles and differential expression/production of these organelle components in response the gut environment. One of the main scientific limitations of the approach is the potential for limited identification of subcellular organelle genes in gut microbiome data. Other possible datasets are not provided to mitigate this risk. The need for NCEMS resources to conduct the proposed analyses are not well-supported. Most analyses, gene identification and differential gene expression, can be done with existing pipelines. Conceptual synthesis between study systems, BMC, ferrosomes, condensates, is limited, i.e., each system is an autonomous analysis using the same dataset. Overall, bacterial subcellular organelles are an exciting research area, and the PIs are respective experts in their systems, but the noted limitations and lack of synthesis between systems in the approach temper excitement around the proposed working group.

title: Discovery and functional analysis of bacterial organelles through mining and refinement of omics data
scientific_merit_and_innovation_justific: The proposal seeks to build on exciting data suggesting bacterial organelles are common and will test how widespread they are across taxa. Basic questions/hypotheses are proposed and will be tested using standard bioinformatics techniques on curated datasets from human gut microbiome samples. It is likely the team will largely be able to answer their primary question of how common the different organelles are within the taxa present in their sample types. Such data may impact the field by revealing evolutionary histories and linkages for organelle synthesis/acquisition.
feasibility_justification: The goal to test regulation of the various organellar elements based solely on snapshot metatranscriptomic, or proteomic, samples is unrealistic with too many caveats to interpret, and no reasonable conclusion could be drawn based on increased or decreased transcripts, or proteins, between sample types based on these limited samplings. DNA sequences will be equally informative to potential regulation. The possibility that divergent sequences may encode organelles will not be assessed. However, their primary goal to identify the prevalence of different organellar types in the samples they are assessing is feasible.
data_sources_and_limitations_justificati: It seems like a missed opportunity that the team wouldn’t look to use other well curated microbiome datasets, e.g., from soil or other environmental samples, to more broadly test their hypothesis.
open_science_compliance_justification: No concerns
overall_rating_summary: The team proposes studying the extent to which bacterial organelles, focused on 4 types, are found across taxa present in human gut microbiome samples. The idea that prokaryotes may possess organelles is an emerging area of research along with the study of the function of said organelles. The assembled team incorporates a number of experts studying bacterial organelles and includes additional team members, including trainees, with expertise in structural biology and bioinformatics approaches. As such, the primary goal of the study is likely to be accomplished as described and will advance knowledge within the field.Concerns are noted as to whether the goals of identifying how expression of the organelle types is regulated is feasible and to the limited scope of the datasets to be investigated, i.e., human gut microbiome only. There does not appear to be consideration for the null hypotheses, but this may not be important at this stage given the “discovery” aspect of the project.
